content:
I'm sharing a multi-agent autoformalization system I built as my final PhD project at Meta.

Using ~30K Claude 4.5 Opus agents, we formalized Darij Grinberg's Introduction to Algebraic Combinatorics (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00738) in Lean over the course of a week. Excluding the exercises, the formalization should be complete. The entire project is shared publicly with source available CC-BY-NC.

  • Autoformaliztion codebase: https://github.com/facebookresearch/repoprover
  • Lean code base: https://github.com/faabian/algebraic-combinatorics
  • Blueprint & side-by-side for targets: https://faabian.github.io/algebraic-combinatorics/targets.html
  • Preprint: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/repoprover/main/auto_textbook_formalization.pdf

While there are many AI formalization announcements lately, a few distinctions for this project:

  • To my knowledge, it's the first fully automatic formalization of an entire textbook.
  • The formalized content is largely disjoint from mathlib (but builds upon mathlib of course)
  • The source text is roughly 10x larger than the Sphere Packing project (with the caveat that this is a textbook, not research papers).
  • Everything is open-source, and we're transparent about compute costs and remaining inefficiencies.

Our approach: mimic what human software developers do with coding agents: git, pull requests, issues, continuous integration, no "secret sauce" anywhere.

We are neither Lean nor combinatorics experts. While we are confident there are no major issues endangering the overall soundness, we have not manually verified all 340 targets. If anyone is willing to inspect the code and share findings on quality issues the autoformalization community needs to tackle, we would highly appreciate it.

Very happy to answer any questions here -- this is not supposed to be yet another flashy PR announcement.

Regarding "Excluding the exercises", I think formalizing exercises is a worthwhile challenge towards useful autoformalization of textbooks. The formalizations of the exercises themselves would not be the goal (they're of no particular use, beyond allowing correction of any mistakes in the exercises that are shown up), so the entire point would be to fill out the sort of API gaps (in both the textbook material and pre-existing mathlib material) that may not be stated explicitly as lemmas in the textbook but turn out to be helpful when applying the textbook material in practice. Of course that needs an autoformalizer that specifically aims to produce a high-quality API that's well-integrated with mathlib rather than producing proofs that work around missing API or contain fragments that would better be factored out to separate API lemmas.

Any plans on upstreaming any of this to mathlib?

As Joseph points out, one key benefit of formalisation is to increase the amount of curated mathematics, i.e., mathematics in mathlib. As Oliver Nash once curtly put it, "Mathlib or it didn't happen". My fear with projects such as these is that there's a chance that the project is now deemed "finished" and a year later it's just sitting there rotting and of no use to anyone other than being a datapoint of what you can do with $100K in one week in March 2026 (answer: 130K lines of code). According to the paper it's $200 per page and $300 per theorem/definition.

Don't get me wrong -- I think experiments like this are great! But one has to also ask -- what is the point of them other than giving data points?

Joseph Myers said:

Regarding "Excluding the exercises", I think formalizing exercises is a worthwhile challenge towards useful autoformalization of textbooks.

It would be nice to have something where the book and the formalized code (or maybe the blueprint), and also the statements of the exercises formalized, but the proofs actually "left as exercise", to be filled by the reader. That would make it a book with "interactive exercises": you can not only do the exercises, but also have them automatically checked for correctness.

Aah yes that would be another interesting outcome -- instead of just the 130K lines of Lean code, how much more effort is it now to make a formal verso blueprint containing both the source file and the lean, with interactive exercises? Given that you have both the LaTeX and the Lean, you have all the ingredients to make a wonderful thing. This would be a really good answer to "what is the point".

Any plans on upstreaming any of this to mathlib?

per Meta policy this is CCBYNC licenced

you'd have to redo the work taking "inspriration"
re exercises, I agree a fully proved API would be the ultimate goal, but that opens two cans of worms while I wanted to focus on one here :)
very happy if anyone would like to play with turning this into an education resource with verso etc!

I think theory development at a lower level of generality than Mathlib is a potential different answer to "what is the point"!

As an example, I used Mathlib's group theory API to do some exercises and theorems in an abstract algebra course (we assigned exercises from Dummit and Foote) and I found it pretty useful in a few instances, especially in surfacing "invisible mathematics" where I felt the textbook proof was too slick and I wanted to see more details. Mathlib's approach to ring theory (where for e.g. Ideal R is defined as Submodule R R) makes it more difficult for me - I understand why it's the right abstraction, but D&F discuss rings, ideals etc before discussing modules, so it's a bit of a disconnect. If someone autoformalized D&F in the order of the book, that autoformalization wouldn't go into Mathlib (for obvious reasons), but I would still find that useful. I wouldn't really need it to be a formal verso blueprint or even have any exercises really - just a formalization of chapters 7-9 that does not mention modules/submodules.

Of course, like in all software engineering, the maintainence challenge remains - how much effort would be needed to keep that hypothetical D&F formalization from bitrotting?

Fabian Glöckle said:

per Meta policy this is CCBYNC licenced

So your claim "Everything is open-source" is actively misleading. CC BY-NC does not meet the terms of the Open Source Definition.
my bad, whats the correct term for CCBYNC? "source available"?
Yes, "source available" is a term commonly used for such cases.

Imagine we are constructing a grand Tower of Mathematics. Lean is our foundational material, and Mathlib serves as the solid concrete structure the community has already built. In this analogy, autoformalizing an entire textbook is like erecting scaffolding around our existing work. While scaffolding isn't a permanent, load-bearing structure itself, it drastically accelerates construction compared to building from nothing. If we find the scaffolding is unstable or misaligned, we can easily dismantle and rebuild it without much cost. We also shouldn't worry if the scaffolding lingers, as long as it helps the community continue building together.

Ultimately, what interests me most is whether we can use this scaffolding to push our construction into entirely new territory—reaching mathematical heights no one has ever explored. I believe that day is fast approaching.

Jinzheng Li said:

without much cost

Nice analogy, but at $100K a textbook, maybe this is not quite the case yet...

@Bryan Wang
$100k isn't really that much, to be honest, and we can reasonably expect the price of tokens to decrease exponentially in the future.

Why does everyone say this? Isn't another possibility that the tech companies get us all addicted to tokens and then the price increases exponentially?

$100K is a lot of money but it would cost more to get humans to do this work and furthermore they'd do it a lot more slowly.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Why does everyone say this? Isn't another possibility that the tech companies get us all addicted to tokens and then the price increases exponentially?

$100K is a lot of money but it would cost more to get humans to do this work and furthermore they'd do it a lot more slowly.

Indeed I think this is likely, at the moment they are in the typical market expansion / venture capital money burning stage, which costs them so much more per token than they charge.

As has been the case with other such situations (Microsoft / Uber, etc) , this honeymoon period doesn't last forever and after consolidation the "enshittification" begins.

But one has to also ask -- what is the point of them other than giving data points?

Obviously upstreaming to mathlib should be explored, but as @Li Xuanji mentions, the goals of a proof as an educational resources vs proof for the ultimate canonical library are slightly different. An analogy in the software worlds would be implementing an algorithm in Python for a algorithms class, and contributing it to the python core library. It first doesn't hurt and puts you on the right track, but ultimately the final result in core python might be unrecognizable, due to the extra constraints the core library has (higher bar for maintainability, performance etc). It might not even be possible due to mathlib design decisions that the education material had leeway on.

Independently, I do enjoy having Lean companions for math textbooks and would love to see many more of those. They can serve an independent from mathlib purpose as companion educational texts. Basically, if one truly wants to push the boundary and adopt Lean proofs as the sole standard for mathematically rigorous proof, then the pdf + lean companion can together become the study material for the topic for future readers:

  • the text provides intuition, narrative text, definitions and proof statements
  • the lean companion provides the formal proofs that follow the text (the semi-formal paper proofs can be skipped) and states exercises.
  • the reader does the exercises in lean
    At least that's how I am using Tao's Real Analysis and enjoying this (with the help of Claude, otherwise the overhead lean proofs being 10x longer than paper rigorous proofs starts to weigh me down).

With verso one can imagine merging the pdf + lean companion, but for a long time most authors will not be adopting lean and an independently overlayed companion by Lean enthusiasts can give support without having to get buy in from the original author.

Questions for the author:

  • how did you pick this particular book. There is only one full text book companion I know of - Tao's real analysis - https://github.com/teorth/analysis. And if you (like me) believe in the value of Lean companions, it would have been more natural to do linear algebra or abstract algebra next (as more core math subjects).
  • why is the repo not structured according to the chapters in the book, I would like to read it chapter by chapter together with the book, but the organization makes it hard.
  • $100K feels on the very high side. My own (very primitive) experiments with formalizing textbooks and lecture notes feel that a lot can be done on a basic $100/month Claude subscription. E.g. I got https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/pages/lecture-notes/ lecture 1 in a few hours.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Why does everyone say this? Isn't another possibility that the tech companies get us all addicted to tokens and then the price increases exponentially?

$100K is a lot of money but it would cost more to get humans to do this work and furthermore they'd do it a lot more slowly.

Because you can always expect some open source/weight models to catch up with the current performance of current SOTA models in few months and the cost to run those open source models are in general low, e.g. Leanstral.

Not a lawyer here, but I don't think copying definitions to Mathlib requires adhering to that license. Too short! I also think, because of the origin of the material, the only claim they can make at all is for the collection (aka database law) as a whole. I wouldn't be worried about that license with respect to taking parts of the work and giving them new places in Mathlib.

Jinzheng Li said:

Because you can always expect some open source/weight models to catch up with the current performance of current SOTA models in few months and the cost to run those open source models are in general low, e.g. Leanstral.

To be fair this is partly because they can distil other models, and that's due to the larger models running at a loss and being cheap enough.

Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

To be fair this is partly because they can distill other models, because the larger models run at a loss and are cheap enough.

That is ture, and I do not think it is a bad thing...

My point was just that the premise is a bit circular, as in saying it's okay if the SOTA raise prices because the open models can distil the SOTA models. But they can only do so because SOTA haven't raised their prices.

@Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦

I see your point, but I don’t think distillation is the only or even the essential reason open models can improve themselves. Moreover, if they truly want to distill a model, the cost of tokens remains far lower than the expense of setting up GPU arrays and training the model.

@Rado Kirov

  • I picked the book specifically so that there's enough content that's not already in mathlib (ruling out introductory subjects) but that it is accessible from mathlib and doesn't require intermediate content)
  • didn't have "textbook companion" usage in mind, for me it was just about getting all the contents into a formal library formalized, and the agents decided on the structure themselves. Should be possible though to refactor if you'd like to give it a try!
  • my prototype system is certainly somewhat wasteful. But first chapters might be a skewed measure, it's a last mile problem of getting the hardest proofs right eventually
What is a "formal library" here? Is it a one-book library?

• I picked the book specifically so that there's enough content that's not already in mathlib (ruling out introductory subjects) but that it is accessible from mathlib and doesn't require intermediate content)

That makes sense, also makes the opportunity to contribute to mathlib larger. I am still not clear what's the principle for what belongs in mathlib and what not. Surely it can't fit all of published mathematical proofs. But can it fit all mathematical proofs that are deemed important enough to be taught as undergrad or grad courses and have an book or lecture notes written (like in this case). And if the answer is no, then we still want to have some healthy ecosystem of maintained non-mathlib but reusable formal libraries of proofs that new research can use, and then your repo becomes useful. But maybe the answer is yes, in which case your efforts would have been better spend aligning the output with mathlib more explicitly?

I am a fan of companion usecase, but it is very nascent and it feels like an awkward compromise - a new text written with mathlib and lean concurrently with the math will always be a better experience.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Why does everyone say this? Isn't another possibility that the tech companies get us all addicted to tokens and then the price increases exponentially?

$100K is a lot of money but it would cost more to get humans to do this work and furthermore they'd do it a lot more slowly.

The main objection is market forces and the simple fact that model parameter size is not really getting bigger. The Frontier Models essentially have Parameter Size on the Order of 1 Trillion. But bigger is not better, its rather smaller is better, along the lines that intelligence is about compressing effectively. One can also observe this trend in open source model sizes.

So given the model sizes are stagnant (or even reducing), and at the same time there is immense value and opportunity to reduce the inference costs of models, we can expect model inference costs to decrease over the long term. There are plenty of hardware / software optimizations, e.g. General Compute Increase, optimized Hardware for LLMs Inference, Better Distributed Systems / Routing, Quantization, Model Distillation, KV Cache Optimization to name some (and then also Proprietary Optimizations). You can even envision AI helping in creating Hardware / Software / Algorithmic Optimizations, which bring costs down even further.

Ultimately we cant pinpoint how much is VC subsidized or how big their current margins are, but its pretty safe to say that over the long term Token per $ (or more generally Intelligence per $) will decrease, the main pressure against the tech oligarchy just upholding margins coming from Open Source Models.

Some Data on Inference Price Trends: https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends/

@Fabian Glöckle , @Vivien Cabannes , can you comment on the cost? Projects like https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07455 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03298 report the cost of $100-200 to formalize a textbook, with O(100k) LOC. Your reported cost is almost 1000x more. What made your project so expensive?

Various things can come into play: difficulty of targets, inefficiency in the pipeline (we messed up with caching and Fabian only applied a 3x discount to be conversative, but I expect it to be rather a 10x discount rate based on our new experiment, meaning the project is probably more 30k than 100k), suscription tends to be more interesting than paying per token if you do not care about speed
A more detailed analysis is beyond what I can provide sadly

if you do not care about speed

they report 24 days, so only 3.5x slower than your project.
Meta pays per tokens, and we do care about being 3x faster

Thanks for raising this. I think the Isabelle and Naproche projects are great additional data points, but to compare carefully:

  • There is no factor of 1000. If we assume the same cached input price as the Isabelle project, the total cost of our project is at $55600 (Table 2, at $25/M output, $0.5/M input), compared to $8900 for the Isabelle project, so a factor of 6x. (We wanted to give an upper bound not to mislead the community, and our API does not report usage in the exact same way ccusage does and the Isabelle project / ccusgae does not seem to require cache write.) The number of $160 is because a subscription was used that subsidizes heavy users. The correct comparison is API pricing.
  • I expect there to be a certain overhead for coordination in parallel setups, so paying 6x more for 3.5x the speed would seem reasonable, if project volume and difficulty are comparable.
  • Comparing by output volume is difficult because it would favor verbose code. (Our review system is specifically designed to maintain reasonably high code quality standards, and there haven't been many complaints from Lean experts regarding the code quality. Review cycles can be expensive and can take several rounds to conclude.) In terms of input volume, the formalized sections from Munkres cover 241 pages while those from our formalization cover 497 pages of Grinberg, roughly 2x.
  • To assess difficulty, note that point-set topology is probably already extensively covered in Isabelle's AFP while we made sure to select a book that is mostly disjoint from Mathlib. It is unclear whether the Claude Code based setup allowed internet access (while we ruled that out with our selection of tools).
  • The Isabelle project reports that it was "83% automated". Our interventions were strictly restricted to a handful or restarts with improved general prompts, efficiency fixes and deletion of the "issues folder".
